title: Dynamic Programming
summary: Count stair-climbing choices by saving smaller answers. Trace a dynamic programming table and reuse its values in six languages.
introduction: Suppose you can climb one or two stairs at a time. How many different ways can you reach the fourth stair? Instead of drawing the same small routes again and again, keep their counts in a notebook. Dynamic programming uses saved smaller answers in this way.
learningObjectives: Build a table of answers from smaller cases
Explain why saved answers prevent repeated work

blocks.text: Dynamic programming solves a problem by reusing answers to smaller problems that come up more than once. The word dynamic does not mean the code changes while it runs. Here we fill a table from the smallest answer to the largest.
ways[step] means the number of step sequences that reach that stair. The final move must be one stair from step - 1 or two stairs from step - 2. These choices are different, so add their counts.
The base answer is ways[0] = 1. There is one way to climb zero stairs: make no moves. That empty plan lets a first move of one or two stairs be counted correctly.

items: Save ways[0] = 1 for the empty plan. For stair 1, only a one-stair move is possible, so ways[1] = 1.
For stair 2, add ways[1] and ways[0]: 1 + 1 = 2. The plans are 1+1 and 2.
For stair 3, add ways[2] and ways[1]: 2 + 1 = 3. These answers are already saved.
For stair 4, add ways[3] and ways[2]: 3 + 2 = 5. The plans are 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 2+1+1, and 2+2.

blocks.text: The same program in six languages

Choose the language you are learning. Each tab solves the same problem and prints the same result. JavaScript can run in this page. The other tabs need separate local tools: a C11 compiler, a C++17 compiler, Python 3, .NET 8 or later for C#, or Java 17. Use Program.cs for C# and Main.java for Java.

variants.code:
n = 4
ways = [0] * (n + 1)
ways[0] = 1
for step in range(1, n + 1):
    ways[step] = ways[step - 1]
    if step >= 2:
        ways[step] += ways[step - 2]
print(ways[n])

blocks.text: The program prints the count 5, not the routes themselves. After the loop, the table holds [1, 1, 2, 3, 5]. Each answer was calculated once and can help the next two answers.

Use a non-negative whole number of stairs. For zero stairs, the program prints 1 for the empty plan. This example counts sequences: 1+2 and 2+1 are different because the moves happen in a different order.
Keep n between 0 and 20 for these cross-language practice programs. The count grows quickly, and fixed-size integer types can overflow on larger inputs. Also, a table of n + 1 values needs memory.
How much work and extra room?

For n stairs, the loop fills n entries and does at most one addition per entry, so time is O(n). A naive recursive method asks for the same smaller counts many times; saving each answer avoids that repeated work.

The table has n + 1 entries, so extra space is O(n). Only the previous two counts are needed to get the next count. Keeping just those two would reduce space to O(1), but the table makes the saved answers easy to inspect.

blocks.title: Try one small change
blocks.text: Change n from 4 to 5. Reuse ways[4] = 5 and ways[3] = 3 to predict 8 before running. The code sizes its table from n, including in C.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not set ways[0] to 0. Zero stairs has one empty plan, not zero plans. Starting at 0 would make every later count zero. Also fill smaller steps first so their answers exist when needed.
